title: Choose words for the situation and your role
intro: I can explain how words change with the listener, situation and job I am doing.
example: A familiar classmate knows the game: “Can I have the next turn?” A new visitor does not know the starting place: “Please stand behind the blue cone to start.” Both are respectful. The second adds information the visitor needs. Neither wording proves a person’s age, authority or background.
steps: 1. Notice context and familiarity
Ask who is talking, what they want to do and what the listener already knows. Respectful language can sound relaxed, helpful or firm.
A classmate asks “Can you help me?” A visitor may need “Could you show me where the library is?” The useful difference is the information and shared knowledge.
Ask for help finding the art room, first from a friend who knows you, then from a new visitor.
Accept clear respectful requests that name the art room and suit the supplied familiarity. Explain a useful change or why the same wording could work. Do not demand one fixed formal phrase.
2. Match language to the interaction role
A host welcomes and guides, a leader explains a task, and a learner may ask for clarification. A person’s role can change during an activity.
Guide: “The reading table is beside the window.” Visitor: “Which window do you mean?” Guide: “The window next to the door.”
Act as the guide, then visitor. Repair “Put it there” when the object and place are unclear.
For example: “Put your bag on the shelf beside the door.” The listener now knows the object and place. Observe the actual exchange; accepting an answer on paper does not establish a spoken tone.
3. Explore cultural choices with the right source
Greetings and respectful expressions vary across languages and communities. Ask what a real expression means, when it is used and who has permission to use a particular protocol.

A Welcome to Country is delivered by Traditional Owners or Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander people with their permission. Anyone can offer a respectful Acknowledgement of Country. These have different roles and purposes.
With an adult, examine an authorised local greeting and an actual protocol example. What context and role fit each?

Use the actual community-approved source and explain its stated meaning or purpose. A greeting used elsewhere is not automatically local. Compare roles; do not imitate a Welcome or invent a ceremony. The retained guide gives concrete adult preparation.
mistakes: “Polite means very formal.”
Natural friendly wording can be respectful.
“A role stays fixed.”
A leader can become a listener or ask for help.
“One cultural greeting fits everywhere.”
Confirm the actual language, community, context and permitted use.
activity: Choose a request for a pencil. Say it to a familiar partner, then to an imagined new class visitor. Swap host and visitor roles, make one instruction clearer and discuss what each listener needed to know.
adjust: Starter: adult supplies the context and a request stem. Core: choose and explain clear wording. Stretch: change roles or repair a misunderstanding while keeping the intended message.
safety: Observe actual communication and record prompts. Do not grade accent, eye contact, social status or a family’s greeting customs. Use verified cultural sources with adult and local guidance.
tricky: 1. Can the same words suit a friend and teacher?
Yes. Explain whether they are respectful and clear in each actual context.
2. Is “please” enough to fix “Put it there”?
No. The listener may still need the object and location.
3. Can any visitor perform a Welcome to Country?
No. Use the permission-bearing protocol roles taught above and local guidance.
faq: Must every response be spoken?
Writing or AAC can support reasoning and communication; record any speech-specific feature not observed.
Where do we find a local greeting?
Start with the school’s approved local First Nations language source or local language centre. Confirm meaning and appropriate use before teaching it.

title: Explain what you appreciate in a text
intro: I can name a response and support a preference with an actual text detail.
exampleTitle: A reason points to something the text does
example: Original lines: “Tip, tap, tiny rain; tip, tap, on the pane.” A response might be “I enjoyed the repeated tip, tap because it reminds me of little raindrops.” The reason connects a real sound pattern to a reader’s response. Another reader can prefer a different feature with a supported reason.
steps: 1. Name a precise response
Use words that say what you liked, enjoyed or found surprising. Name the actual setting, character, image, word pattern or event.
Original story: “Lia’s paper boat tipped. She folded its sides again. At last it floated in a shallow tray.” “I liked Lia’s persistence” means I appreciated that she kept trying.
Give a response to the supplied story and point to a detail.
For example: “I enjoyed the ending because Lia’s next try works.” Accept another supported response, including dislike. Teach unfamiliar response words such as persistence before relying on them.
2. Explain a preference and compare it
A preference chooses one option over another. A relevant reason explains the choice, rather than simply repeating that it is good.
Text A: “The little boat bobbed beside the bank.” Text B: “The boat moved.” Both describe a boat. One reader prefers A because bobbed gives a particular up-and-down movement.
Which version do you prefer for a story, and why?

Accept A for its more particular movement or B for a reason suited to the reader’s purpose, such as a very simple caption. Liked, enjoyed and preferred do not form one fixed strength scale; preferred usually needs a comparison.
3. Appreciate words specific to Country and Place
Use the actual text and its supplied language guidance. Explain what a particular word adds to the setting, keeping its language and creators identified.
Adult supplies Cooee Mittigar by Jasmine Seymour and Leanne Mulgo Watson. Read a real spread and its glossary. In this Darug source, Nura refers to Country and yana to walking.
Choose a word or setting detail actually read. Explain how it helps you appreciate that particular Country or invitation.

Refer to the real page and glossary, and accept different supported responses. Do not replace the actual book with an invented cultural passage, assume a local translation, or judge the child’s pronunciation from printed words alone.
mistakes: “I liked it” explains everything.
Add the feature and why it mattered to you.
“Everyone must prefer the same text.”
Different supported preferences are valid.
“Any reason fits.”
Check that the reason matches a real text detail.
activity: Read the original rain lines in the worked example. Each partner shares a preference or response, points to the relevant words and gives a reason. Compare what each noticed. For the cultural focus, use the actual prepared book and glossary.
adjust: Starter: choose between two response stems with an adult. Core: name a feature and relevant reason. Stretch: compare two texts or explain why a partner’s different response is also supported.
safety: Adult read-aloud supports access but is not independent decoding evidence. Personal preferences are not right or wrong; check the link between response and actual text.
tricky: 1. Is “because it was good” very specific?
It repeats a judgement. Explain which feature worked and why.
2. Must an excited response use the word exciting?
No. Explain the feeling and the text detail in natural words.
3. Can an unfamiliar cultural word be guessed from an illustration alone?
Use the authorised text, glossary and guidance; an image is not a reliable translation dictionary.
faq: Do I need a long review?
No. One clear response, relevant reason and actual detail can be useful.
Can we discuss a text we disliked?
Yes. Use respectful, specific language and evidence rather than judging another reader.
modelCaption: Name the feature and its effect

title: Compare how texts are organised for a purpose
intro: I can explain how order and language help different texts do their jobs.
exampleTitle: The same topic can have different jobs
example: Story: “A seed rolled into a dragon’s boot. The dragon shook it out and planted it.” Procedure: “Plant a seed. You need a pot, soil and a seed. Put soil in the pot. Place the seed in the soil. Water it.” Both concern a seed, but one tells imagined events and the other guides actions in order.
steps: 1. Compare connected events and grouped information
Narratives often introduce characters and a setting before connected events. Recounts tell events in time order. Information texts group related facts. These are common patterns, not rigid tests.
Recount: “Yesterday we visited the garden. First we planted a seed. Then we watered it.” Information card, heading Seeds: “Some seeds grow inside fruit. A seed can grow into a plant.”
Which tells a past class event, and which groups facts about seeds? Give an order or language clue.
The recount uses Yesterday, we and ordered events. The information card groups seed facts under a heading. A text can mix purposes, so explain the actual evidence rather than sort by topic alone.
2. Connect organisation, language and form
A procedure orders actions; an opinion can state a choice and reason. The same purpose can appear in different forms, such as a poster, email or brochure.
Opinion message: “Please keep our reading corner quiet so everyone can enjoy a book.” Procedure: “Fold the paper. Draw a star. Open the paper.”
How would the order change if the supplied procedure cards were mixed? Could the opinion be sent in an email?
Keep fold before drawing on the folded paper, then open. Yes: an email could carry the same opinion and reason. A poster is a form, not automatic proof of persuasion.
3. Notice how a response refers to poetry
A response can name a feeling, quote or identify a feature, and explain the connection. Poetry may use repeated sounds and line breaks instead of a story problem.
Original poem: “Tip, tap, tiny rain; / Tip, tap, on the pane.” Response: “I enjoyed the repeated tip, tap because it reminds me of raindrops.”
What is the response doing that the poem itself is not?
It explains a reader’s reaction to a feature of the poem. The repeated words support that reason. Do not require all poems to rhyme or every story to have the same opening words.
mistakes: “Topic tells the text type.”
Compare the job, order and actual language.
“One clue proves the purpose.”
Use several clues from the complete text.
“All stories and poems follow one pattern.”
Use common patterns thoughtfully and check the real example.
activity: Read the six complete samples in More examples. Choose two, explain a shared topic or feature and one organisational difference. Reorder the actual three paper-flag cards, then explain why the actions need that order.
adjust: Starter: compare two adult-read examples. Core: explain purpose, structure and language clues. Stretch: put the same opinion in a different form and explain what can stay the same.
safety: Use the complete supplied samples or actual texts, including all relevant pictures. Adult reading supports comparison; no genre label by itself demonstrates comprehension.
tricky: 1. Does numbered writing always give instructions?
No. Numbers can order events or facts. Read what the sentences do.
2. Must an opinion be a poster?
No. It can appear in an email, brochure or other suitable form.
3. Can a poem response include a reason?
Yes. A reader can connect a particular feature to a response.
faq: Are these fixed recipes for every text?
No. They are useful common patterns to compare with actual examples.
Why use texts from different learning areas?
The purpose changes: reporting science observations, explaining a maths method and telling imagined events can need different organisation and language.
modelCaption: Look at what the text does
modelCards: Response: what did I notice and why?

title: Link ideas with clear references and omissions
intro: I can track who or what words mean and recover words left out of a clear context.
exampleTitle: Keep the person and the owned thing clear
example: “Mia found her hat. She put it on. The hat was hers.” Her, She and hers refer to Mia; it refers to the hat. The words connect the sentences without repeating Mia and hat every time. If another person could be meant, use the name again.
steps: 1. Track personal and ownership words
A personal pronoun can stand for a person or thing. Ownership forms connect an item to its owner. Use the whole context, not just the nearest noun.
“The eggs were in a bowl. Jo moved them carefully.” Them refers to the eggs, not the bowl. “Jo found his bag. The bag was his.” His refers to Jo in this stated example.
In “Ava has a kite. It is hers”, what do It and hers connect to?

It refers to the kite; hers shows that it belongs to Ava. Accept an explanation that restores the complete meanings: the kite is Ava’s. Do not infer anyone’s pronouns from a name alone; follow the supplied text.
2. Restore words understood from context
Sometimes words can be left out because the reader can supply them. Restore the words first to check that the shortened text keeps the meaning.
“Alex chose red paint. Sam chose blue.” The second sentence means Sam chose blue paint. In “Who watered the seeds?” “Jo did”, did stands with the understood earlier action.
Expand the reply in “Who packed the bag?” “Nell did.”
“Nell packed the bag.” The earlier question supplies the action and object. This kind of omission is different from writing three dots; not every incomplete phrase is made clear by leaving words out.
3. Repair reference when needed
Choose pronouns or omissions only when the intended meaning remains clear. Related words can track a person in different roles, but not every related noun names the same person.
“Mia met Ava. She carried the bag.” She could mean either person. If Ava carried it, write “Ava carried the bag.”
Repair that draft if Mia carried the bag. Explain why the repair helps.
“Mia met Ava. Mia carried the bag.” The repeated name removes the ambiguity. Repeating a noun is useful when it clarifies meaning; removing every repeated word is not the goal.
mistakes: “A pronoun means the nearest noun.”
Check number, meaning and the wider text.
“Every repetition should disappear.”
Repeat a name when it prevents confusion.
“Any missing word is understood.”
Restore it from the actual surrounding text and check.
activity: Use the complete Mia, Alex and Jo texts in More examples. Draw arrows from reference words to their people or things. Expand one shortened reply. Rewrite one unclear sentence with the intended name supplied.
adjust: Starter: adult highlights a name and its replacement. Core: track personal/ownership forms and restore an omission. Stretch: explain two possible readings of an ambiguous reference, then choose a clear revision.
safety: Reference tasks concern meaning in the supplied text. Allow spoken explanation, arrows, AAC or writing. A grammar label is useful only when the child can explain what the word connects to.
tricky: 1. Does hers replace a name alone?
It expresses an owned thing belonging to the person identified in context, such as Ava’s kite.
2. Is leaving paint out always clear?
Only when the surrounding text supplies the intended paint meaning.
3. Can a repeated name be the best choice?
Yes. Clarity can matter more than avoiding repetition.
faq: What does cohesive mean?
The parts of a text connect so a reader can follow the meaning.
Do we need advanced ellipsis terminology?
No. Show the understood words in a short familiar text and explain how the reader recovers them.

title: Find information in books and on screens
intro: I can choose a useful route, follow it and check the information I reach.
exampleTitle: Contents and an index answer different needs
example: In the prepared mini-book below, the contents list gives “Feeding a rabbit — 8”. The index gives the more specific “Water — 8”. The supplied printed page 8 says water is in the white bowl in this class model. Page numbers guide the search; reading the destination checks the answer.
steps: 1. Use chapter and contents order
A chapter is a section of a book. The contents list shows its sections in book order and where they begin. Choose a broad heading that fits the information need.
Use the complete prepared contents and page extracts below. The chapter numbers 1, 2 and 3 are different from the printed page numbers 3, 8 and 14.
Which chapter and page begin information about feeding? Check the supplied page extract.
Chapter 2, Feeding a rabbit, begins on printed page 8. The actual extract discusses the model’s feed and water bowls. The number 2 names the chapter, not its page.
2. Use an alphabetical index
An index lists specific terms, usually alphabetically, with page references. Check later letters when two terms start alike, then follow the correct reference.
For the same mini-book, Bedding comes before Bowls: after B, compare e and o. Cleaning, Home and Water follow in alphabetical order. The page extracts are in focus 1.
Find the specific term Water and use its page reference. Which bowl holds water in this model?

Water points to printed page 8; the white bowl holds it in the supplied model text. Do not guess from a heading alone. On an actual PDF, printed page numbers may differ from the viewer’s sheet counter.
3. Navigate and verify on screen
A side-bar lists routes; a drop-down or expandable menu reveals choices; a link moves to a destination. Use its label, then check the heading and actual information.
The prepared website below has a real Topics menu and real links. It uses native controls and stays on this page.
Open Topics, follow Food and bowls, then follow its link to Home and bedding. What does the final section say?

The final heading is Home and bedding; fresh bedding goes in the model’s sleeping area. Observe actual menu/link use, then return to the menu. Naming a link or drawing a route alone does not demonstrate navigation.
mistakes: “Chapter number equals page number.”
Read the contents columns carefully.
“Contents and index are identical.”
One follows section order; the other usually sorts specific terms alphabetically.
“A click finishes the search.”
Check that the destination answers the original need.
activityTitle: Find three things and explain your routes
activity: Use the actual prepared book extracts to find the feeding chapter, water-bowl colour and bedding location. Then use the native screen menu to visit both topics and return. Explain why each chosen route helped.
adjust: Starter: adult models one route. Core: locate a chapter and specific index term, then follow real links. Stretch: compare two routes to the same information or explain a printed-page/viewer-counter mismatch.
safety: This is a prepared teaching model, not complete rabbit-care advice. Use adult-approved websites for further navigation. Observe actual book or screen actions without a speed race.
tricky: 1. Must an index follow chapter order?
No. Its terms are usually alphabetical, even when their page references jump around.
2. Does a menu label prove the answer?
No. Open the destination and check its information.
3. Can two routes reach the same page?
Yes. A broad contents heading and a precise index term can point to the same chapter.
faq: Can a paper website drawing show screen navigation?
It can help plan a route, but observe the actual screen action separately.
What if the first route is unhelpful?
Return, choose a more useful heading or term and check again.
modelCaption: Follow the route all the way to information

title: Connect complete ideas in a compound sentence
intro: I can join complete ideas and explain the relationship between them.
example: “The bell rang” and “The children lined up” can each stand as a complete sentence. “The bell rang, and the children lined up” joins them and adds the second event. A conjunction such as but, or or so would express a different relationship; choose the one that fits your intended meaning.
steps: 1. Find two complete clauses
An independent clause can stand as a complete sentence. In these examples, it names who or what and tells something complete about them. A nearby group of words may still be incomplete.
“The dog barked” is complete. “Under the table” names a place but does not tell a complete event. “The dog and the cat” names two animals but gives no action or state.
Are “The gate opened” and “The dog ran out” each complete? Explain.
Yes. Each names its subject and tells a complete event. Contrast “ran out” alone, which does not identify who did it in this independent sentence check.
2. Choose the relationship
And adds an idea, but contrasts, or offers a choice, and so introduces a result. More than one conjunction can be grammatical while giving a different meaning.
“The path was wet, so we wore boots.” Wetness is the supplied cause; wearing boots is the result. “I wanted to play outside, but it was raining” contrasts a wish with the situation.
Join “The room was noisy” and “We moved to a quiet table” to state a result.

“The room was noisy, so we moved to a quiet table.” Keep cause before its stated result. And would add the second event without making the result link as explicit; it is not the requested relationship.
3. Build and reread the whole sentence
Keep both clauses complete, join with the chosen coordinator and check capitals and final punctuation. Use a comma before the coordinator in these demonstrated two-clause models.
“I wanted to read. The room was too noisy.” Joined for contrast: “I wanted to read, but the room was too noisy.” A comma alone would not supply the intended conjunction.
Does “The dog ran and barked” show two independent clauses in this lesson’s model? How could you make two explicit clauses?

It has one stated subject with two linked actions; and alone is not proof of a compound. “The dog ran, and it barked” makes two complete clauses explicit. Different grammar analyses can discuss understood subjects; use the demonstrated primary convention consistently.
mistakes: “Every and makes a compound.”
Check whether it joins words, actions or complete clauses.
“Any conjunction keeps the same meaning.”
Name the intended addition, contrast, choice or result.
“A comma alone joins every sentence.”
Use the taught joining structure and reread for meaning.
activity: Use the complete clause cards in More examples. Join two related clauses for a stated relationship. Change the conjunction and explain how the meaning changes. Include one fragment card and explain why it cannot stand alone.
adjust: Starter: adult reads two complete clauses and names the relationship. Core: join them and explain the coordinator. Stretch: create a three-clause compound or repair a confusing connection while preserving the intended facts.
safety: Judge complete meaning and the requested relationship. Open combinations can have several valid answers when no relationship is specified; do not reject a grammatical option merely because it differs from a model.
tricky: 1. Is “red and blue shoes” a compound sentence?
No. And joins describing words in a noun group, not complete clauses.
2. Can a compound have more than two clauses?
Yes. Three or more complete clauses can be coordinated.
3. Does so always mean a result?
No. In “so big” it intensifies a description. Here we study so joining a cause to a result.
faq: Must we memorise every coordinating conjunction now?
No. Build understanding with useful familiar and, but, or and so before expanding.
Is every different conjunction wrong?
No. It may make a grammatical sentence with a different relationship. Follow the stated task and explain meaning.
modelCards: The bell rang, and the children lined up.

title: Build useful noun groups and verb groups
intro: I can add helpful noun details and find the whole verb group in a sentence.
exampleTitle: Find both groups in the whole message
example: “The small brown dog was barking.” The noun group The small brown dog names the animal and gives useful detail. The verb group was barking tells about its action at that time. Was belongs with barking; brown describes the dog, so it is outside the verb group.
steps: 1. Extend a noun with helpful words
A noun can name a person, place, object or idea. Articles such as a, an and the and adjectives can extend the noun group. Choose details that fit.
“A tree” can become “a tall tree”. “The dog” can become “the small brown dog”. In “Kindness matters”, kindness names an idea rather than a physical object.
Build a noun group around kite using an article and accurate describing words.
For example, “a bright red kite”. Accept another sensible group. The main noun remains kite, and the extra words identify or describe it; adding more adjectives is not automatically better.
2. Find the whole verb group
A verb can express an action or state. A verb group can include a main verb and helping words. Read the full sentence to see which words work together.
“The children are running.” The whole verb group is are running. “The bird has finished.” Has finished is the whole group. “The ball was touched.” Was touched works together.
Find the whole verb group in “The girl was painting”. What does the helper add?
Was painting is the group. Was helps place the ongoing painting in past time. Do not leave out the helper or include girl, which belongs to the noun group.
3. Compare what the added words do
Ask useful questions: how many, what kind, or what is it like? Keep noun details connected to the noun, and make verb forms fit the intended sentence.
“Two pairs of old walking shoes” specifies quantity, condition and type. “The parrots are calling” needs are for the plural subject; “The parrot is calling” uses is for one.
Improve “The bird flew” with a useful noun detail and a suitable two-word verb group.

For example, “The small bird was flying.” Accept another clear sentence and explain the meaning change. A switch from flew to was flying changes how the action is presented; it is not merely a longer copy.
mistakes: “Every nearby word is in the noun group.”
Check what identifies or describes its noun.
“Only the action word is the verb group.”
Include helpers such as was or are when they belong.
“Longer groups are always better.”
Choose accurate details that help the reader.
activityTitle: Build a sentence with two groups
activity: Use the article, adjective and noun cards in More examples. Build one sensible noun group, add a suitable verb group and read the whole sentence. Swap one word and explain the changed meaning or grammar.
adjust: Starter: adult highlights a noun and a verb. Core: build a useful noun group and identify a whole verb group. Stretch: compare quantity or time changes in two clear sentences while keeping vocabulary familiar.
safety: Use complete actual sentences. A child can point, colour, speak, use AAC or write to explain grouping. Do not score drawing or handwriting instead of grammatical meaning.
tricky: 1. Is brown part of was barking?
No. Brown describes the dog; was barking is the verb group.
2. Must every verb be a physical action?
No. Verbs can also express states, as is does in “The child is happy”.
3. Does an always come before a word starting with a vowel letter?
Choose a or an by the next spoken sound, including any adjective. For example, an old tree and a small tree.
faq: Do noun groups need many adjectives?
No. Use only useful, accurate details.
Does a two-word verb group always mean now?
No. Compare is running, was running and will run in their complete contexts.

title: Combine what words and images tell you
intro: I can explain what an actual image adds and check an inference against visible clues.
exampleTitle: A picture can supply an unstated place
example: Words: “The kitten waited.” The actual illustration shows a kitten under a wooden chair in a room. Together they suggest it waits indoors under the chair. The words alone do not say that location. Neither the picture nor the sentence tells us its name, how long it waits or a certain hidden feeling.
steps: 1. Separate written and visual clues
Read the actual words, then inspect the actual image. Name what each supplies before combining them. Treat an inference as supported thinking, not certainty.
Use the kitten image below with the word line “The kitten waited.” Visible chair legs, floor and walls support the indoor setting.
What does the illustration add that the words do not state? Can you know why the kitten waits?
It adds the place under a chair indoors. The reason for waiting is not supplied. A story writer could invent one, but label it as a new story detail rather than observed evidence.
2. Read information from a real graphic
A table or map can add facts that a short sentence leaves out. Read the headings, labels and values together.
Words: “Some seeds sprouted.” The supplied class table records the same week: tray A has 2 visible shoots; tray B has 5.
What extra information does the table give? Which tray has more visible shoots in the record?
It identifies each tray and gives its count; B has 5 compared with A’s 2, so B has more in this record. The table does not prove why the difference occurred or predict every future tray.
3. Explain action, reaction, speech and thought
Pictures can show poses or facial clues. Speech and thought bubbles use visual conventions to add spoken or unspoken meaning. Check exactly what is shown or authored.
Use the first story duck in the actual three-panel image below. Its step and open smiling bill can suggest a cheerful action. The separate bubble diagrams add two original possible story meanings.
Compare the supplied speech bubble with the thought bubble. How would each change the story?

The speech bubble makes “Come and read with me!” spoken to someone. The thought bubble represents “I wonder what we will read” as unspoken thinking. These are explicitly new diagram choices, not text already inside the reused artwork. Accept other evidence-supported reaction readings; do not claim a face proves one feeling.
mistakes: “Every picture is decoration.”
Check for added location, action, reaction or information.
“An image proves a hidden feeling.”
Explain visible clues and keep an inference qualified.
“Labels alone are enough.”
Inspect the actual image, table values and words together.
activityTitle: Words first, then the complete picture
activity: Read “The kitten waited” with the image covered. Say what you know. Reveal the real illustration and name two added visible details. Compare those observations with one possible inference, then explain what remains unknown.
adjust: Starter: adult points to one visible clue. Core: explain how words and image combine. Stretch: compare the duck’s speech/thought choices or explain a question the seed table cannot answer.
safety: Use the actual supplied visual, with panning where needed on a small screen. Verbal descriptions and alt text support access but are not claims that an absent picture was inspected. Accept accessible ways to explain evidence.
tricky: 1. Can you tell the kitten’s name from this picture?
No. No name is supplied.
2. Does the seed table explain the cause of different counts?
No. It records counts for the stated trays and week.
3. Is a thought bubble necessarily spoken aloud?
No. In this model it shows unspoken thinking, while a speech bubble shows spoken words.
faq: Must every text-image pair repeat the same information?
No. Images can add information, suggest a response or alter how the words are understood.
Can readers give different interpretations?
Yes, when each explains actual clues and distinguishes observation, inference and invention.
modelCards: Visible place: under a chair indoors
Unknown: name, reason and waiting time

title: Choose vocabulary that fits the topic
intro: I can try a more precise word and explain why it fits the intended meaning.
exampleTitle: Precision depends on the actual context
example: “The character spoke very quietly so the baby would not wake.” Whispered fits this stated soft speech. Shouted would change the action. A more precise word helps only when it matches the intended meaning; a long or impressive word can be a poor choice.
steps: 1. Learn a topic word in context
Ask what the word names and how it fits the surrounding information. Explain it in everyday language before using it.
A thermometer is a tool for measuring temperature. In a temperature report, thermometer can replace the vague word thing when that is the actual tool used.
Choose a precise word for the tube carrying water to plants in a garden, using the supplied meaning: a hose is a flexible tube for carrying water.
Hose fits this context. Use the full sentence, such as “Water flows through the hose.” Do not choose a specialised word merely because it belongs to science; it must name the intended object.
2. Compare character and action words
Different nouns, adjectives and verbs can create different pictures. Check the actual character’s action and the writer’s intention.
“Nell hesitated at the doorway and spoke softly” can support timid, meaning shy or hesitant. “Nell shook when she heard the frightening noise” more directly supports frightened.
In a story about a character racing to catch a rolling ball, would strolled or hurried better fit the intended movement? Explain.

Hurried better matches moving quickly to catch it. Strolled suggests a more relaxed movement. Accept another accurate word with a reason; use actual context rather than a universal ranking of stronger words.
3. Choose words with their source and Country identified
First Nations language words can name particular places, actions or ideas. Learn from a verified creator or community source and keep that context clear.
For the Darug text Cooee Mittigar, adult uses the actual book and glossary. The publisher identifies Nura with Country and yana with walking in this source.
With the prepared book open, choose an actual topic word and explain its meaning using the glossary. Would you assume the same word is local everywhere?

Refer to the actual source and identify its language and creators. No: confirm local language and permitted use separately. The aim is a meaningful word choice with attribution, not an invented translation or a pronunciation quiz.
mistakes: “Choose the longest word.”
Choose the accurate word that helps your reader.
“A related topic word always fits.”
Check its exact meaning in the sentence.
“A cultural word is interchangeable everywhere.”
Keep its particular language, source and Country clear.
activityTitle: Try a word and explain the difference
activity: Use the actual garden and story paragraph in More examples. Replace one vague noun, verb or adjective with a word that fits the supplied context. Read both versions and explain the meaning gained or changed.
adjust: Starter: adult explains two word choices with a sentence. Core: choose and justify a fitting word. Stretch: compare two valid choices for different intended effects or revise an overprecise unsupported description.
safety: New vocabulary should be explicitly taught. Accept a clear everyday choice when it serves the purpose; do not reward unfamiliar language just for sounding advanced. Use actual approved cultural sources.
tricky: 1. Does hurried always improve went?
No. It adds quickness, which must fit the intended action.
2. Are timid and frightened exact synonyms everywhere?
No. They can describe different responses; use the actual clues.
3. Can nice be useful?
Sometimes. If a particular detail matters, explain what is pleasant, peaceful or helpful instead.
faq: How can we check a new word?
Use a reliable dictionary or the source’s glossary, discuss its context and try it in a complete sentence.
Must a new story word be factually true?
In fiction, a writer may invent details deliberately. Distinguish that choice from describing evidence in an existing text.

title: Use title capitals and clear list commas
intro: I can follow a stated title style and separate complete items in a list.
exampleTitle: State the title style before editing
example: For this title-case model, capitalise the first word and main words: “A Walk to the Pond”. Internal to and the stay lower-case. Sentence case is another valid style: “A walk to the pond”. Both keep the first word capitalised and preserve proper-name capitals. A title task must tell you which convention to follow.
steps: 1. Notice capitals in actual titles
Identify the work’s name and follow the given model. Title styles vary; capitalising every word is not a universal rule. Proper names keep their capitals.
For these exercises, use title case: capitalise the first word and main words; keep internal a, an, the, and, or, to and of lower-case unless part of a proper name.
Edit the title “mia and the moon” using this stated style.
“Mia and the Moon”. Mia is a name, Moon is a main title word, and internal and/the remain lower-case in the given model. A task without a declared style should allow a valid consistent alternative.
2. Separate whole list items
Find each complete item before adding commas. Use commas between listed items and and before the final item. Do not separate the words inside one item.
Items: a red hat / two blue pens / a ruler / paper. Model: “We packed a red hat, two blue pens, a ruler and paper.”
Add commas to “We saw ducks hens and goats.”
“We saw ducks, hens and goats.” Also accept a clear serial-comma version, “We saw ducks, hens, and goats”, unless a stated style excludes it. Keep the full stop.
3. Edit for the reader’s meaning
Check title boundaries, proper names and the whole list. Reading aloud can help notice grouping, but commas are not simply marks for every breath.

Draft title and sentence: “a trip to canberra. We took a sun hat a red bag and water.” In the stated title-case model: “A Trip to Canberra”. The list sentence is “We took a sun hat, a red bag and water.”
Create a title using the given title-case model and a sentence listing three complete items. Explain one capital and one comma.

Accept a title following the declared model and a clear three-item list. Credit appropriate name capitals and either clear serial-comma convention unless a style is specified. Do not split a multiword item.
mistakes: “Every title word must be capitalised.”
Follow the chosen style and keep name capitals.
“Every pause needs a comma.”
Find grammatical groups and actual list boundaries.
“A two-item list always needs a comma.”
Two simple items usually use and without a separating comma.
activityTitle: Make and edit a reading card
activity: Write an original title using the stated title-case rule and a sentence listing four things needed for its story. Mark each whole list item, then insert commas and final and. Swap with a partner and explain the changes.
adjust: Starter: adult models one title and a three-item list. Core: apply the stated title style and separate whole items. Stretch: compare sentence case with title case, or edit a list containing multiword items.
safety: Use familiar words and proper names with confirmed spellings. Do not mark an unstated style preference as the only correct answer. These exercises concern title capitals and list commas, not every use of punctuation.
tricky: 1. Is A Walk to the Pond the only valid way to style that title?
No. It matches the declared title-case model; sentence case can also be valid in another context.
2. Should a comma split red hat?
No. A red hat is one complete item.
3. Does a list sentence still need an end mark?
Yes. List commas do not replace the sentence’s final punctuation.
faq: What is a serial comma?
It is an optional comma before the final and in a list under some styles. Use the stated convention or accept a clear consistent alternative.
Why compare actual book titles?
They show how capitals identify names of works and how publishers’ styles can vary.
modelCaption: Use the stated convention and preserve each item
